items.en: I can share certain things, but some things are private and are not my story to tell. I don’t know all of the conversations between the two of them. I can say there were struggles, but those conversations were private between R.J. and me and between him and his friends. She moved in December, and they had only seen each other three or four times since then. I don’t know what those conversations were after she moved. I had not spoken with her about not coming to the funeral. She had asked one of R.J.’s friends on the day I found my son, but at that point we didn’t even know what was happening. No plans had been made. That’s all I can share about it.

His grandparents also had a strong influence. I grew up with a grandmother who was a children’s minister and a mother who worked in education. When R.J. and his sister were young, we gave them allowances and asked them to set aside 10 percent as a tithe and another 10 percent in a charity bank. Every Christmas, they chose a child from a giving tree, Make-A-Wish or another organization and spent that money on the child they had selected. They learned that because they were fortunate, they needed to give back. They learned to recognize that other people might be less fortunate and to lend a helping hand.

That passion carried into his acting and advocacy. He spoke out for actors with disabilities and worked with organizations including Shriners Hospitals for Children and United Cerebral Palsy. He raised money, spoke around the world and advocated for inclusion and diversity in the workplace and education system. He believed everyone should have the opportunity to audition for a role, whether it was written for a disabled character or not. He fought hard for that. He wanted to change the world and make it better for everyone.

I think we’re talking about two different stars. He was a star, but I’m talking about the shining star in the sky. What makes someone a celebrity or a star? R.J. never believed he was better than anyone else. He never identified himself as a celebrity. He simply loved acting and loved working with producers. Vince Gilligan allowed him to shadow different departments on Breaking Bad, and R.J. learned about every part of filmmaking — the producer, director, cinematographer, actor, lighting, camera and everything else. He understood that great things happen when people work together.

We don’t have all the details worked out yet. Because R.J. worked so diligently in South Texas, we knew we needed to have something there, and it was an incredible day. The building reached maximum capacity, and the city opened an overflow building that also reached capacity. After calls came in from Los Angeles, New York and around the world, we knew we needed to do something somewhere else. Los Angeles seemed like the logical place because so many people who wanted to attend were there, including directors, producers, actors and crew members who had worked with R.J.

Those closing down the carpet included Heated Rivalry‘s Connor Storrie, Teyana Taylor, Jodie Turner-Smith and the Kardashian-Jenners, who have a tradition of wrapping up the event every year. This time, Kim Kardashian and Kendall Jenner stopped for photos while Jenner’s boyfriend Jacob Elordi stood back and recorded video of her posing on his phone. After the famous sisters had cleared the step-and-repeat, Elordi quickly stood his own images before meeting up with the group again — out of sight of photographers (at least until they got inside).

Also present was much of the Academy Museum Gala host committee, which included Jessica Alba, Judd Apatow and Leslie Mann, Autumn Durald Arkapaw, Adrien Brody and Georgina Chapman, Jon M. Chu, Kirsten Dunst, Nicholas Galitzine, Ludwig and Serena Göransson, Regina Hall, Kate Hudson, Jessica Lange, Greta Lee, John Legend and Chrissy Teigen, Rami Malek, Demi Moore, Olivia Munn, Gina Prince-Bythewood, Questlove, Da’Vine Joy Randolph, Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen, Bird Runningwater, Elliot Grainge and Teyana Taylor.

Eminem has defended his decision to collaborate with longtime friend Kid Rock, after their new team-up drew backlash from some fans over the two artists’ opposing politics.

The rapper appears on “Heal My Faith,” a track from Kid Rock’s new faith-based album Halfway 2 Jesus, released Friday (Oct. 17). Hours after the album arrived, Eminem addressed the pairing on social media. “Not about choosing sides, just choosing to make music with my old friend,” he wrote. “Praying for all of us.”

The collaboration had surprised some of Eminem’s fans given the two Detroit artists’ well-documented political differences: Eminem endorsed Kamala Harris at a 2024 Detroit rally and has criticized Donald Trump on tracks including “Campaign Speech,” while Kid Rock is among Trump’s most prominent supporters in music. Eminem addresses that divide directly in his verse. “From shock rap to the rock rap, my homie and me / He is my brother, not my political enemy,” he raps, before calling for unity across party and religious lines.

Kid Rock, who has been friends with Eminem for roughly four decades, spoke about the collaboration in an interview with Billboard. “I really didn’t want to drag him into my political world,” he said, adding that the two discuss politics “a little bit, not a ton.” He described the album as being “about forgiveness and second chances” and an attempt to “heal some of the division in our country.” Kid Rock also noted that Eminem was initially announced for a different track, “7 Sins,” before the two decided to keep their collaboration to a single song; that slot ultimately went to Lil Wayne.

The two have a long history together. Eminem featured on Kid Rock’s 1998 song “F— Off” from Devil Without a Cause, and Kid Rock appeared in the video for Eminem’s 2013 single “Berzerk.” Both rank among the best-selling artists in Billboard history — Eminem has notched 10 No. 1 albums on the Billboard 200 and five No. 1 hits on the Hot 100, while Kid Rock broke through with his diamond-certified 1998 breakthrough Devil Without a Cause and scored a Hot 100 top 10 with “All Summer Long.”

NEW YORK, Oct. 18 (UPI) -- Weapons, Resident Evil and Euphoria actor Austin Abrams says the role of a grieving son who finds himself in the literal belly of a beast was exactly what he was looking for when he auditioned for Whalefall.

"It's just so insane. It was something that I wanted to do, something that I'd never seen before and something that I would want to see and something that felt like an extreme challenge to make," Abrams recently told the crowd at New York Comic Con.
"It was a challenge to make for everyone involved. We had one of the best crews I've ever worked with and, for them, they were constantly figuring out, 'How are we going to do this?'" he said.

"Also, the emotional, personal story that's at the heart of it was just so moving and, then, that tied in with the whale and I just found the whole thing so mythogical. I just found it really compelling. I couldn't NOT do it."

The adaptation of Daniel Kraus' best-selling novel follows Jay Gardiner (Abrams), who is swallowed by a massive sperm whale while trying to find the remains of his estranged father Mitt (Josh Brolin) who died by suicide.
Directed and co-written by Brian Duffield, the film co-stars Jane Levy, Emily Rudd, Elisabeth Shue and John Ortiz.

"I read the book when I was in Italy doing Ridley [Scott's] movie Dog Stars and rarely have I slowed down purposefully when it comes to the end of a book, because I didn't want it to end. Then, for some reason, which I still don't totally understand, when I got to the end of the book, I put it to my chest and I sobbed," Brolin recalled.

"I knew I was in when I finished the book and, then, ultimately, Brian and I talked and, then, when I knew Austin was in it, having just done Weapons with him, I knew it would be a party of discomfort and I couldn't wait."
Kraus said that, of the 30 books he has written, this is the one he least expected to be adapted as a movie.

"What inspired it was that, to a lesser extent, it happens and I don't mean the swallowing part, but divers or kayakers, usually, do end up in the mouths of these humpback whales. You can watch the viral videos," Kraus explained.
"That's what inspired me. I saw one of those videos. I thought, 'Is there actually a way that some whale out there could swallow someone and, if so, is there a way that they could survive?'"
Kraus contacted whale scientists, who informed him that sperm whales have enormous throats that could, theoretically, make the story he wanted to tell possible.

"Then I started a three-month course of advanced whale studies, trying to figure out what exactly could someone do inside the stomach," the author said, explaining he didn't want to tell a fantastical whale tale like Pinocchio or Jonah. "My only interest was doing it scientifically, biologically accurate."
The term "whalefall," as described by Kraus, is used when a whale dies and begins to decompose in the deepest, darkest part of the ocean, creating "shock waves" for other sea life and animals.

"That became, to me, a really powerful metaphor of the death of anyone, the death of any loved one you've ever had. They die, but their life radiates out from their death for generations," Kraus said.
Duffield said: "I thought it was going to be really super-competitive and everyone was going to want it. So, then, I was really hounding Daniel and then I was the lone lunatic."

Oct. 18 (UPI) -- Hurricane Trudy was expected to begin veering away from Mexico's central Pacific coast on Sunday, while still bringing rains and gusty winds to the region, the National Hurricane Center said.
The eye of the hurricane was about 115 southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico, and 165 miles west of Manzanillo, Mexico, the National Hurricane Center said in its 8 a.m. CST update.

It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, making it a Category 2 storm on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, and was moving northwest at 8 mph, the forecasters said. It grew slightly in strength compared to Saturday afternoon.
A tropical storm warning was in place for Las Islas Marias and along the coast from Playa Perula to San Blas.
The storm was forecast to turn northwestward Sunday, the NHC said.
"On the forecast track, the center of Trudy will start moving away from the coast of mainland Mexico this afternoon and then move south of Baja California Sur on Monday and Tuesday," it said.

Trudy was expected to produce 2 to 6 inches of rainfall with isolated higher totals of around 12 inches through the weekend along the coast of Jalisco. The NHC said the rainfall might produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Elsewhere, its outer bands were expected to produce 1 to 2 inches with isolated higher totals around 4 inches along the southwestern coast of Mexico in Colima and Nayarit.
Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 30 miles from the center of the storm and tropical-storm-force winds extended outward up to 105 miles.

Oct. 18 (UPI) -- Police arrested more than 2,000 people across more than 100 locations in France as weekend protests turned violent, resulting in damaged buildings, fires and vandalism, authorities said Sunday.

In a post on X on Sunday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said more than 600 government authorities, including police officers and firefighters, were injured in protests throughout the country Saturday. He said "several hundred" businesses sustained damage and/or looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, Limoges and elsewhere.
Sky News reported that the 140-year-old town hall building in Limoges was set afire Saturday night, causing it to collapse.
Alexandre Bompard, the president of the Retail and Trade Federation, said protesters caused "several hundreds of millions of euros" worth of damage to hundreds of shops.
There have been varying reports about how many people took part in Saturday's protests, ranging from the 550,000 cited by police, to 800,000 reported by organizers.
Nuñez said officials were investigating to identify the perpetrators involved in Saturday's violence.
"Protesting is a fundamental right," he said in the post. "Sowing disorder with violence and in a coordinated manner is not."
The Guardian reported that one person involved in the protests died of a heart attack.

French President Emmanuel Macron was expected to deliver a public address in response to the protests, which began a month ago led by students frustrated by teacher shortages, crowded classrooms, decaying facilities, exhausting schedules and lack of funding. The protests have spread throughout Europe, also taking place in Belgium, Albania, Greece and Italy.
Macron was scheduled to begin his address around 8 p.m. CEST. In a post on X on Saturday, he expressed support to police and promised to punish the violence.
"Those who have ransacked, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished," he wrote.

There are gifts for men. And then there are manly men gifts. Countless gift guides for the men in your life offer up the same neckties and tool sets and tasteful leather belts. And don't get us wrong: We're classy people, too. We like only the finest T-shirt a Savile Row tailor recommends, and anything themed for whiskey.

But this is a guide to the manliest gifts made for man men, menly objects ranging from the most classic of man totems to the most ridiculously hypermasculinized. Welcome to the red-hot tropics of the manosphere. Mere regular soap will not do when soap with the word “men” on it also exists. No mere shaving for us, when shaving can be aggressive. Enjoy.
For more men-themed gifts for man-themed men, check out our Gifts for Outdoorsy People, our Gifts for Dads Who Don't Need Anything, and Gifts for Golfers.
Updated October 2026: We've added a toiletry bag from SPC/LST, a pressure washer, a head shaver, and a giant flashlight; removed a couple sold-out options; and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

- A Cannon for Pepper Shaking isn't manly. Grinding is manly. Cannons are manly. Grinding so dominantly that your pepper grinder can plausibly be called a cannon is manly. So is deftly tooled precision of any kind. But Männkitchen’s Pepper Cannon isn't an expensive gimmick for the insecure. Its stainless steel burrs will grind peppercorns to the exact right size, among 50 settings, and this will end up mattering to anybody who spends a lot of time seasoning meat or building a rub. The all-metal construction will last decades. And it'll grind your pepper so fast it'll feel like the Dust Bowl got spicy.

- Bourdain’s Favorite Knife Every man needs a good knife. Probably two. One for his pocket. One for the kitchen. If you're going to get a good knife, why not Anthony Bourdain's? Maybe it's me, but I pretty much don't know a dude who doesn't have a tattered copy of Kitchen Confidential somewhere in his house. This Global 8-inch chef's knife is Bourdain's knife, the one he recommended to starting chefs. The one he recommended as a baseline good chef's knife for those at home. It is Japanese-made stainless steel, ice-hardened, lightweight. Seamless from its handle to its convex edge. The Global chef knife is economy itself. It is a knife that most chefs own eventually. Maybe the man in your life would also do with a good knife.

- Lasers for Measuring Everything You know what men like? Knowing how long something is, or how far away it is. Know what they (I) don't like? Stretching out a dinky tape measure that keeps shimmying or bending or snapping back into the roll. The solution to everything is always lasers. Lasers can do anything. Just ask Elon Musk. Anyway, just point this Mileseey S50 at anything, press the button, set your starting measuring point, and it'll tell you how far away it is. (It measures to 1/32 of an inch, but I wouldn't trust it past 1/16 of an inch.) Get a tripod for it and you can also do point-to-point measurements from a distance. I've measured windows for fittings. Door jambs. Most of the rooms and spaces in my house. I've barely used tape for four months. Why use tape when you can use lasers? Mileseey says the green laser light on this S50 is more visible than red light during the daytime. Maybe this is true. There are also a whole lot of trigonometric functions I haven't figured out, and the included instructions are only half helpful. But mostly I just want to know: How big is that thing? How far away?

- A Tactical Toiletry Bag A Real Man (™) is always mission-ready, whether he’s rappelling off a cliff or heading into the hotel bathroom to brush his teeth. That’s why he needs a multipurpose pouch made of water-resistant 600D Cordura Re/Cor. The military-inspired System Kit from SPC/LST features two sections that can snap together (one zips flat and has three internal pockets, while the other zips only on the top and has just one zippered pocket), along with a 20-mm side strap with a clip in case you need to attach it to your pack, truck, or parachute. —Kat Merck

- The Manliest Grill Gloves Nothing is manlier than overkill. Lots of grill gloves can take a little heat, and save you from a hospital visit on a grill day. But can they take you to the gates of hell? These Hell Hands grill gloves from Big Green Egg are rated up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They're made with thick cowhide that goes most of the way up to your elbows—and look like something you'd wear for the zombie apocalypse. The pads are made with thick, puncture-resistant Armortex fabric and stitched with Kevlar. I don't know if this makes these gloves bulletproof. But what I do know is that I have placed my palm flat onto a scalding 500-degree cast-iron pan while wearing one of these Hell Hands. I barely felt warmth, let alone heat. These gloves are monsters. But note that these gloves are thick enough that your hands will feel more like mittens than hands. You'll need to use manly finger strength to flex them.

- The Most Tactical Pants These pants are the most tactical pants of all pants, according to WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson. Cargo pants look like a baggy bouquet of pockets. But these pants? They are for men of action. They are stretch canvas, svelte, sturdy. They have pockets inside other pockets, pockets that remove traces of being pockets. If you're the sort of guy who wants to look good, without looking like you want to look good, these pants are your pants.

- An “Ultra-Tough” Cooler You might wonder whether black is the most natural color for a cooler, given its propensity for absorbing heat. OK, and? Suck it up, and embrace the steely, Vader-esque manliness of this Ultra-Tough cooler from RTIC. It's roto-molded, natch, but it's also filled with 2.8 inches of foam. I have tested the 45-quart version while tailgating in temps where the cooler was actually helping keep our seltzers from exploding. The Ultra-Tough is a beast to carry by yourself (the manly way, the way John Wayne would carry a cooler) because it weighs almost 30 pounds empty. This means it's about 55 pounds with a 24-pack of Bud Light, and 60 pounds if you toss in a 5-pound bag of ice from the store. But the foam handles mounted on free-swinging ropes make it manageable. In terms of build quality, this RTIC cooler is actually a little more solid than the Yeti size 65 that I previously owned, especially when it comes to the leak-free screw-in drain plug. —Martin Cizmar

- Beef in a Box Pat LaFrieda is a New York butcher. His dad was a butcher, and his dad's dad was a butcher, and so was the dad before that. The first butcher became a butcher after he got in a fistfight outside a butcher shop. This is Naples, Italy, we're talking about, where you sell meat or you are the meat. (We made this proverb up, but it seems right.) Anyway, this is not just good but actually great beef in a box. Pat LaFrieda beef is the beef served at some of the most famous restaurants in New York. It will also come in the mail, wherever you are: fresh, never frozen. And then it goes on the fire. According to WIRED meat delivery guide boss Scott Gilbertson, smart people wait for that super-fresh beef with a catcher's mitt, then cook it right up. Beef this good, you don't make it wait.

- The Manliest Jacket Waxed canvas is a manly fabric. A working man's fabric. It sheds water like a senator sheds consequences. But unlike politicians, this jacket builds character over time. It becomes itself. It'll build your character, too—or at least make you into one. After all, this is the jacket Pedro Pascal wore in The Last of Us, worn and rubbed down until it became shades darker. Because this is what silent, manly men wear, and wardrobe people know this. And sure, this Flint and Tinder trucker's jacket doesn't breathe quite as well as boring, unwaxed cotton. It resists everything except compliments.

- A T-Shirt for the Strong and Stout An American man gathers bulk over time. It is the burden he carries, like the weight of responsibility or the consequence of bacon. Anyway, this shirt is made for the stout at heart (and maybe middle) but strong of arm. It hugs the biceps and chest, showing off raw power. But unlike a lot of T-shirts, it doesn't blouse out like a 1950s nightshirt. It's a man's shirt. For men who are a lot of man. A reliable white T-shirt, and a black T-shirt, are needed by pretty much all men.

- For Super Soft Brillo Beards If you put words Amazon doesn’t like in a product’s name, that immediately makes it more manly. To wit, there’s Duke Cannon’s Best Damn Beard Oil, for scratchy facial hair. This beard oil helps prevent ingrown hairs and makes facial hair feel softer to the touch. Though, please note, the bottle says explicitly that it’s “not for clowns,” so don’t buy this for any Pagliaccis in your life. —Eric Ravenscraft

- For Powerful Coffee Just look at that name: Moccamaster. This is a coffeemaker that drinks and breathes pure power and precision. The Technivorm Moccamaster is burly, yet precise. It makes old-school drip coffee, better than that fancy Starbucks stuff. But what the manly man in your life should truly love about the Moccamaster is that it’s real hand-tooled craftsmanship. It is perhaps the world’s only high-end coffee maker that looks like a power tool made by DeWalt, and it is just as sturdy. It’s been handmade since 1968 in the Netherlands, a country where their idea of a party is often just blowing things up. The precision-made Moccamaster will keep your coffee within a four-degree range for optimum brewing. And its parts can be replaced or repaired, just like the engine of an old car. Judging from others’ experience, it’ll probably last you decades. What a machine. Moccamaster.

- A Pressure Washer Cleaning something outside? Garden hoses are for girlie men. You need 2,600 pounds per square inch of water pressure dispensed from a tank on wheels. This model even comes in nature's natural warning colors: black and yellow, like a wasp. The 35-foot cord ensures you'll be able to cover plenty of territory, which is important because this Home Depot–exclusive set includes a FOAM CANNON for cleaning your F350 Super Duty, side-by-side, or wakeboard boat. It looks considerably less impressive in person than it sounds, and the foam produced plays fast and loose with the definition, but still: FOAM CANNON. —Kat Merck

- A Man-Powered Espresso Maker Are you still using electricity to make espresso? Pressing buttons? Go off-grid. Pump your own instead. The Flair is a man-powered espresso machine, with a large lever that lets you self-generate the 9 bars of pressure needed to make good espresso. There's a chamber for your grounds. There's a chamber on top of that for hot water. Fill them up, and pull down on the handle—using a pressure gauge for a guide like the gauge on a High Striker carnival strongman game. Thick, crema-topped espresso will result. Want to double up on muscle? Here's my favorite hand grinder, the Kingrinder K6 ($109), for perfect espresso powder.

The generative AI revolution hasn’t been kind to Vanniall, an OnlyFans creator who lives in New York City. She now constantly finds hyperrealistic deepfakes—AI-generated images and videos that copy everything about her—circulating online and often isn’t able to get them removed.

On top of that, Vanniall struggles to build an audience on popular social media platforms, like Instagram, without getting in trouble. “There’s always some sort of report or appeal that I'm going through with them,” she tells WIRED. Vanniall’s Instagram account, which has over 100,000 followers, is currently restricted and cannot be viewed without logging in.

So, when I tell her that Meta allows its AI agent, called Muse, to engage in explicit sexting with adult users, she seems frustrated by the decision: “It's not fair that they get to pull money out of people with their sexually active AI agent, but they won't let real people, real adults, engage in any sort of sensuality or sexuality.”

It’s a common refrain I heard from other adult content creators, who questioned why their accounts on Meta platforms often seem restricted, while Meta’s AI agent is now allowed to talk dirty with millions of adult users.

“A private, one-to-one conversation between an adult and an individualized AI agent on a platform restricted to people 18 and over is very different from the marketing and promotion of services on a social media platform,” Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton tells WIRED.

Meta’s Muse is the first always-on AI agent to break out of early adopter circles in San Francisco. The Muse app is like a message thread; text the digital assistant, give it access to your personal data, like calendar and email, and have it proactively find ways to help, like canceling a workout class that overlaps with your dinner reservation. Meta’s large distribution network, through platforms like Instagram and Facebook, helped catapult the app to the top of the download charts during its first month, as millions of new users experimented with an agent for the first time.

In addition to having it organize your calendar, Meta says, it’s OK for users of the adults-only app to engage in X-rated AI conversations with Muse. A Meta spokesperson previously told WIRED the company wouldn’t “block legal adult behavior.” Meta’s Muse generates explicit text but not images or videos.

“I think we're already seeing AI being allowed to do more than humans would get away with,” says Jiz Lee, who runs an OnlyFans account and has worked for years behind the scenes in queer porn. Meta has previously flagged Lee’s Instagram posts for removal. Lee feels like queer and trans people are often treated unfairly by large social media companies, whether or not the person is an adult content creator.

Lee traces many online censorship issues back to FOSTA-SESTA, a law signed by President Trump in 2018 that impacted Section 230 protections for platforms, and many websites responded by censoring adult content. “If sex work was decriminalized, then a lot of these issues wouldn't be happening, a lot of the censorship wouldn't be happening,” they say.

Lee also wants to know more about how Muse was trained and who, if anyone, was compensated by Meta for their data. “We've been slow to react industry-wise,” they say. But Lee is starting to see more adult content companies clarify AI usage stances in official contracts. They want to protect performers from being gobbled up into AI training data.
For many OnlyFans creators, navigating Meta platforms is frustrating but critical to remaining visible online. Genius claims to be on his seventh Instagram account in the past five years.

When asked about Muse’s sexting ability, he questioned why Meta made one of its apps, Muse, gated for those 18 and over but doesn’t seem interested in creating another adults-only space on social media. “It could be: Instacam,” he says.

Muse generating adult content could offer explicit AI interactions to a wider audience. Genius says he would be open to collaborating with a tech company to create an AI-version of himself that fans could message. He wants to find ways for humans to keep making money as adult performers, ensuring they aren’t cut out or unfairly trained on. Right now, he sees his human-ness and authenticity as central to connecting with audiences.

Meanwhile, Vanniall is fervently against using any AI agent. Well, at least, Meta’s Muse. “Stop downloading that app,” she says. “You do not need to give Meta any more money or any more of your personal information. They have enough.”

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.

The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “What is a Data Center?,” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.”
"Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks.

The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying, job creation programs, tax breaks, companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies, the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried.

Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools.

“A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says.

In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy.

Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.”

The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools, it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools, it offers data center-themed coloring pages, instructions for an evaporation-themed science project, and print-out activities like “Draw a picture of the cloud" and “Draw a data superhero.” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “Polly Packet's Precious Payload,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers.

7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers.

Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students.

Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.

Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.”

Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.)

Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend.
Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says.

“You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.”

It’s common for companies to sow goodwill through public outreach, and as tech companies have reckoned with the backlash to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment.

A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools.

Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit.
Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas.

Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says.
“As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.”

Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side. When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor.

Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it!

Thursday’s debate between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson was interrupted by a protester yelling about the environmental impact of data centers. Collins tried to use the moment to score points as the more anti-data center candidate, though her finances might indicate otherwise.

Though there’s been a slight recovery to end the week, it reflects increasing skittishness around the data center buildout. Bloomberg also reports that CoreWeave’s founders have sold $3.3 billion in stock since the company went public.

To the untrained eye, the photograph’s pale sky, hazy light and blue-grey foreground could have been snapped in one of Earth’s many desert landscapes. But the panorama was captured millions of miles away from our planet, on a world whose nickname stands in stark contrast with the neutral tones of the image: Mars.

Indeed, NASA’s Curiosity rover used its Mastcam to snap the six images that make up the landscape on August 11 at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, which scientists then stitched together after the rover sent them back to Earth. The final product presents the most detailed view scientists have ever had of wind-carved Martian cliffs, including crags known as yardangs.

"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky,” Ashwin Vasavada, a planetary scientist and the Curiosity project scientist, tells Reuters’ Will Dunham. “But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades of blue. It's like Earth, but it's definitely Mars.”

The yardangs sit on the northwest side of a three-mile-tall mountain called Mount Sharp, and both features sit in Mars’ Gale Crater, according to the outlet. Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012 and has been climbing Mount Sharp since 2014. On August 26, it reached 0.6 miles of elevation, which is a record for Martian rovers.

Mount Sharp’s layers preserve materials from different periods of Mars’ history. Their analysis has shed light on the lakes and streams that existed there billions of years ago, when the Red Planet hosted a much wetter environment. When the water dried up it left behind layers of minerals, and when the deposits stopped accumulating on Mount Sharp, wind possibly eroded the yardangs into being.

However, “the yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” Vasavada says in a NASA statement. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.” In fact, the yardangs don’t seem to be part of the rest of Mount Sharp’s layers, Vasavada adds to Reuters.

Scientists are aiming for Curiosity to reach the base of the yardangs in 2027. When it launched in 2011, the rover was the largest and most capable ever sent to Mars. Curiosity’s objective is to understand if Mars could have ever hosted extraterrestrial microbes, and the rover made headlines earlier this year when it discovered organic molecules that represent the building blocks for life.

Mars “had all the conditions for life to start there when life was starting on Earth,” Andrew Coates, a planetary scientist at University College London’s department of space and climate physics, told the Guardian’s Hannah Devlin at the time of the discovery. “There’s no known reason why it shouldn’t have started on Mars as well.”
Did you know? The many instruments of Curiosity
NASA's Curiosity rover on Mars was built with multiple tools and cameras.
- The Mastcam sits at about human height and is designed to take wide panoramic shots of the Mars surface
- MAHLI, the Mars Hand Lens Imager, provides close-up views or Martian rocks and dust.
- Spectrometers analyze the chemical makeup of substances found on the Martian surface.

Curiosity isn’t the only rover on the Red Planet, however. NASA’s Perseverance also recently made the news after setting a new record for the farthest distance any vehicle has ever driven on the surface of an extraterrestrial world, according to a statement by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory JPL) at the California Institute of Technology.

"Perseverance builds on the 29-year legacy of our past Mars rovers,” Steven Lee, deputy project manager at the JPL, tells Will Dunham in a different Reuters article, “Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity—each incorporating prior lessons and improving our ability to drive on another world.”
After more than two centuries—spanning ten British monarchs, 45 prime ministers and two world wars—London’s oldest restaurant is entering a new chapter.

Rules, a storied restaurant on Maiden Lane in Covent Garden, has changed hands only three times since opening its doors in 1798. Now, J.P. Mayhew, the building’s proprietor for the past 40 years, is donating the site, along with the art collection it houses and rent from the restaurant business, to the National Trust, a British conservation charity, per the Independent’s Emily Beament. Altogether, the donation is valued at £11 million, approximately $14.5 million.

“Rules is [a] place of living history where kings, writers and politicians have dined. A place where you can see, smell and taste not only treacle sponge, but centuries of history, care and memories. A place where cultural traditions have been kept alive, and continue to thrive, despite the world around it changing,” Hilary McGrady, director-general of the National Trust, says in a statement posted to social media.

The restaurant is located on a cobblestone road in the center of London’s vibrant theater district. Over the years, it has played host to countless authors, playwrights and stars, including Charles Dickens, William Makepeace Thackeray, H.G. Wells, Charlie Chaplin, Madonna and Harrison Ford.

In all that time, Rules developed a reputation for discretion. Edward VII, who served as king of the United Kingdom between 1901 and 1910, had a private door built into the restaurant’s paneled walls so he could slip in unseen with his mistress, the socialite and actress Lillie Langtry, according to the Telegraph’s Craig Simpson.

Author Graham Greene even memorialized the restaurant’s romantic potential in his 1951 novel, The End of the Affair. “Is it possible to fall in love over a dish of onions? It seems improbable and yet I could swear it was just then that I fell in love,” Greene’s narrator muses.

Rules has survived crisis after crisis, staying open even during World War II. In those years, service ran for only two hours, during lunchtime, and complied with government rationing guidelines. Those wartime meals “weren’t exactly high gastronomy,” but Rules skirted the strictest restrictions by selling wild-caught grouse, pheasant and rabbit, CNN’s Chris Dwyer reported in July. To this day, Rules sells more game than any other restaurant in the country.

Rules’ cluttered walls are a testament to its history. The restaurant’s four stories are adorned with visitor books, caricatures, portraits and signs. Many of its artifacts bear the faces and names of the high-profile guests who have warmed the restaurant’s plush chairs. Langtry even gave Rules a signed portrait of herself to thank the restaurant for its tactfulness, per the Independent.

While Mayhew is donating the restaurant’s historic building and contents to the National Trust, he sold the restaurant business to Ricky McMenemy in 2022. Under the new arrangement, McMenemy will become a commercial tenant of the National Trust.

The Maiden Lane building will be the first in National Trust’s portfolio to house a running restaurant operation. But the charity is no stranger to historic businesses. Its portfolio includes 39 historic pubs and several country house hotels, according to the Guardian’s Esther Addley and George Francis Lee.
Day-to-day operations of the restaurant will remain under the purview of McMenemy. “It will always be run as a restaurant,” National Trust national curator Lucy Porten tells the Guardian.
McMenemy tells the Independent that the donation gives him and his staff “security and peace of mind” to know that Rules will be looked after even as the restaurant industry weathers instability.

The charity is looking to add ways to expand access to the historic restaurant, potentially through virtual visits. In the meantime, patrons can expect the same rabbit rillettes, pork cheeks and steak and kidney pies. For anyone worried the National Trust may warp Rules with its afternoon tea sensibilities, fear not. “There will be no scones,” Porten tells the Guardian.
Wildlife officials in Australia are taking a hands-on approach to combating the deadly and highly contagious bird flu strain H5N1.
Veterinarians and biologists have just begun a multi-week pilot project to capture and vaccinate shy albatrosses on a remote Tasmanian island.

So far, the albatrosses have remained healthy and free from the virus. However, the avian flu recently reached Tasmania for the first time, and it has sickened dozens of birds from other species since then. Wildlife experts consider the shy albatross highly vulnerable to the H5N1 strain, so they’re taking steps to protect them.

Officials hope the results of the pilot project will inform their broader efforts to combat the avian influenza “at a population level” in the species, Sheryl Hamilton, a wildlife biologist with Tasmania’s Department of Natural Resources and Environment, tells Kelsey Reid of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).

The shy albatross is a large seabird that breeds on three islets in the Bass Strait between the Australian mainland and the island state of Tasmania: Albatross Island, Mewstone and Pedra Branca. They’re considered “near threatened” by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and “vulnerable” in Tasmania. The total population includes an estimated 15,000 breeding pairs.

If all goes to plan, officials hope to vaccinate up to 100 shy albatrosses on Albatross Island, giving each bird two doses of the vaccine. Afterward, they plan to keep an eye on the birds using remote cameras and follow-up visits to see how they respond.

The process is labor-intensive. Wearing head-to-toe hazmat suits, wildlife biologists pick up each bird by hand, weigh it and administer the first dose of the vaccine. They then mark the birds with temporary, nontoxic paint and place numbered markers at their nests to keep track of which individuals are part of the project. They plan to return in a few weeks to administer the second dose.

Vaccinating wild birds is difficult because they’re hard to catch and constantly on the move, making it challenging to recapture them for a second dose. However, shy albatrosses provide a “unique opportunity,” since they can be safely approached multiple times while nesting and monitored “in a way that’s not possible for many wild species,” Guy Barnett, the Tasmanian minister for environment and climate change, says in a statement.

Veterinarians have also been vaccinating little penguins against the bird flu on Phillip Island and St Kilda beach in Victoria, Australia. The squat, black-and-white birds don’t fly, and they return to the same spot each night, making them relatively easy to catch for both doses. So far, more than 1,500 birds have received their first dose.

In 2017, biologists airlifted artificial shy albatross nests to Albatross Island in a bid to boost the species’ breeding success. Warmer and wetter weather, driven by climate change, had been making it harder for the birds’ natural nests to stay together, biologists said.

Tasmania recorded its first official case of the bird flu in August, when a brown skua found on the island’s northwest coast tested positive. Since then, the number of bird flu “events”—in which the virus is detected in one or more animals—has risen to 50, with a Pacific gull, a great crested tern, a little penguin and a black currawong among the latest species affected by the virus, reports Olivia Hicks for 7BU. The virus has not been detected in commercial poultry or backyard flocks, and Tasmania has not experienced any mass mortality events.

Australia had been the only continent without avian influenza until June, when the virus was detected in wild seabirds in the state of Western Australia. Since then, the bird flu has sickened a variety of seabirds and mammals on the continent and its surrounding islands, from greater crested terns to long-nosed fur seals. The virus has also been detected in endangered Australian sea lions and urban foxes.

Across Australia, officials have recorded 706 total bird flu events at last count. Officials are concerned about the spread of the virus in Australia and New Zealand, which are home to many vulnerable species found nowhere else on Earth.
The situation is “quite frightening,” Rachael Gray, a veterinary pathologist at the University of Sydney, tells ABC’s Jacinta Bowler and Peter de Kruijff.
“It’s pretty overwhelming at the moment,” she adds. “These animals, who we very much love and admire and respect … these animals are getting sick, they are suffering and then they are dying.”

Aging is one of the biggest risk factors for developing glaucoma or cataracts — but as scientists look more closely at what happens to the eyes over a lifetime, they are finding that people's exposure to air pollution also plays a role in whether they develop these eye conditions.

Glaucoma, which affects about 80 million people worldwide, is a group of diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It can lead to permanent vision loss, usually affecting peripheral vision at first and later central vision. Cataracts are even more common, affecting more than 94 million people globally; the condition occurs when the eye's lens becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision and, eventually, blindness.

Aging raises the risk of both diseases, as do certain medical conditions, such as diabetes. But now, a review of 41 studies suggests that people who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution may also face a greater risk of these diseases. The research, presented in September at the 44th Congress of the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons in London, brought together evidence from dozens of studies collectively involving millions of people across East Asia and the U.K.

The studies were observational, meaning they can only draw a link between air pollution and the eye conditions, rather than prove that air pollution causes the diseases. But still, "this reframes glaucoma and cataract as conditions shaped by where you live and breathe, not just how long you've lived," said study co-author Dr. Ahmed Alnabihi, an ophthalmologist at King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital and Research Center in Saudi Arabia, who presented the findings. These environmental exposures may compound age-related decline in the eye as they do in cardiovascular disease, he said.

The researchers examined exposure to several pollutants, including different sizes of particulate matter (PM), such as fine PM2.5 and larger PM10. They also looked at nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ozone and carbon monoxide.

Most studies included in the review estimated people's long-term exposure based on the pollution levels around their homes and in their communities. They used a range of methods, including government monitoring systems, satellite data and computer models designed to estimate pollution levels. A few studies examined short-term exposure and its relation to more sudden eye issues, such as acute angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency that can quickly cause vision loss.

Using this wealth of data, the team compared pollution exposure with rates of glaucoma, cataracts and age-related macular degeneration (AMD), another common eye condition that impairs vision. PM2.5 — tiny particles that measure 2.5 micrometers or smaller — showed the clearest associations with glaucoma and cataract risk.

People with the highest exposure to PM2.5 had 70% higher odds of glaucoma, compared to those with the least exposure. Plus, an increase in PM2.5 exposure equivalent to the difference between the 25th and 75th percentiles of exposure within each study was associated with 8% higher odds of glaucoma and a 4% higher hazard of cataracts.

The evidence was less consistent for air pollution and age-related macular degeneration, which damages the central part of the retina that's responsible for sharp, detailed vision. And unlike the clear connection seen with PM2.5, other pollutants showed less consistent links to eye disease. For instance, nitrogen dioxide was not significantly tied to AMD, ozone was not tied to cataracts, and neither pollutant was linked to glaucoma. Sulfur dioxide and PM10 showed no significant associations with any of the three conditions.

The association between PM2.5 and glaucoma was relatively consistent across the reviewed studies, said Nidhi Singh, an environmental epidemiologist at the IUF-Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine in Germany, who was not involved in the study. The findings for PM2.5 and cataracts were moderately consistent, albeit more variable than the glaucoma data; still, she said that the analysis seems to support a link.

Singh did caution that the underlying evidence is observational. "Therefore, the results demonstrate an association, not by themselves a causal effect of PM2.5 on glaucoma or cataract," she told Live Science.

The exact biological mechanisms behind these links remain unclear, but Alnabihi noted that fine particulate matter is small enough to be absorbed into the body. This can trigger oxidative stress, in which harmful molecules overwhelm natural defenses and cause damage. It also drives chronic, low-grade inflammation, in which the immune system stays mildly activated for long periods, he explained.
In the eye's lens, these processes can "damage the crystallin proteins that keep it transparent, causing them to misfold and cloud, which is what a cataract is," Alnabihi said.

In the optic nerve, the same processes are thought to damage retinal ganglion cells, a special type of neuron that relays information from the retina to the brain. This can contribute to glaucoma independent of internal eye pressure, he said, which is another big risk factor.
"Unlike the lungs or gut, its [the eye's] surface is in direct, continuous contact with outdoor air, giving pollutants a uniquely direct route that might cause damage," he added.

Other studies have found clues that support the link between PM2.5 and eye damage. Mice that were exposed to ambient PM2.5 for nine months developed elevated pressure inside their eyes, a glaucoma risk factor. The researchers observed both oxidative stress and nitrative stress — a similar phenomenon — in the tissues that drain fluid from the eye, which may help to explain the rise in pressure.

Studies of humans and human cells have uncovered similar patterns. In data from more than 480,000 people in the UK Biobank, a large repository of health information, those exposed to higher PM2.5 were more likely to develop glaucoma over time. In another study, scientists exposed lab-grown human retinal tissue made from stem cells to PM2.5. The particles disrupted retinal cell development, including that of retinal ganglion cells, while increasing cell death.
These studies offer pieces of a possible mechanism, but for now, how those pieces fit together in people remains unclear.

When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes.

The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317.

This was followed by the Black Death, an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century.

The Black Death era is the perfect opportunity to look at the effects of humans on biodiversity over a longer period, Jonathan Gordon, a paleoecologist at the Leverhulme Centre for Anthropocene Biodiversity at the University of York and first author of the paper, told Live Science.

In the study, which was published March 4 in the journal Ecology Letters, the researchers compared more than 100 European pollen records that included about 4,600 samples. The records came from sites ranging from the lowlands of France and uplands of the southwest United Kingdom to the Swiss Alps.
The pollen records "give us information on the past diversity of the plant records," Gordon said.

For example, cereal grains — such as wheat, barley and rye — were a fundamental part of medieval agriculture. The representation of pollen from these types of crops in the pollen record points to historic land use.

The researchers divided the pollen data into three categories based on the presence of cereal pollen: places where agricultural production went up, places where it went down, and places where there was no evidence of cereal cultivation.
"We found a decline in biodiversity overall, but the decline overall was driven by those landscapes that declined in agricultural production," Gordon said.

"In those landscapes where agricultural production went down, there was a reduction in biodiversity of around 40%. Then, after about 150 years, as populations started recovering and landscape disturbances started increasing again, biodiversity went up to slightly above the level it was before."

Many people think there was a "stable and pristine world in which the entry of people has only one result: net loss of species and homogenization," Erle Ellis, an agroecologist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "The paleoecologists have always known the story is far more complicated."

There is a growing body of evidence showing that people's long-term cultural shaping of their landscapes often creates more diverse habitats, known as "mosaics," that can sustain more species than simple homogenous landscapes can, he said.
Whereas modern agriculture focuses on single crops on plots of land, in previous centuries, "you had all these different types of agriculture operating within the same landscape," Gordon said.

"In that landscape, you had lots of natural features that remained from the Middle or Early Holocene (which began after the last Ice Age about 12,000 years ago)," he added. "You had old bits of woodland, you had heaths, you had ponds, and bits of secondary forest. It was all interlaced with these agricultural mosaics, and that led to raised biodiversity because there were more habitats for different plant species to exploit."

The findings highlight the differences between medieval and modern land use practices — and their consequences for biodiversity. Research suggests that during the 20th century, global biodiversity declined by up to as much as 11% and human activities, such as land-use changes, pollution, and climate change, are the major culprits. In agriculture, the practice of monoculture — where a single crop species is grown over a large area — reduces biodiversity.

"What this work contributes to showing is that, until relatively recently, even in Europe, very different forms of land management and interaction were practiced than exist today," Patrick Roberts, director of Department of Coevolution of Land Use and Urbanisation at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, told Live Science in an email.

"Rather than the monoculture, plantations, or uniform changes to landscapes we see in the 20th and 21st centuries, emphasis was placed on maintaining 'mosaics,'" said Roberts, who was not involved in the new research.

In the study, "we can see how relationships between people and biodiversity have changed through time and how people can actively use landscapes while maintaining biodiversity and mixed ecosystem functions," he said.

There is still more to understand about how humans' disappearance from landscapes in the Black Death era affected the natural world, Gordon said. "There are a lot of other types of diversity — not just the number of types, but what the different types present actually do." There may be a hundred types of plants in a landscape, but if they do the same thing, "you have low functional diversity," he said.

Functional diversity "is super important for how ecosystems adapt to changes in climate and how resilient they are, which is something we need for future-proofing our agricultural system," Gordon said.

Where it is: 7,500 light-years away, in the constellation Cassiopeia
A mysterious "guest star" recorded by medieval astronomers nearly 850 years ago has revealed new secrets after scientists obtained the clearest images yet of its explosive aftermath.

New observations of Pa 30, thought to be the leftovers of a historic supernova called SN 1181, show that its spectacular firework-like filaments are not smooth streams of material. Instead, they consist of chains of tiny gas knots.

SN 1181 is so called because astronomers in China and Japan recorded its brief appearance in the year 1181, when they saw it as a naked-eye object in the constellation Cassiopeia. Eight surviving texts date its appearance to between Aug. 4 and 6 of that year. The mysterious object remained visible for 185 days.

"It's rare to get this level of detail on a supernova we can date to a specific week in history," Timothy Cunningham, an assistant professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of Warwick who led an international team of researchers to study the object, said in a statement.

SN 1181 is one of only five supernovas in the Milky Way galaxy known to have been witnessed from Earth before the invention of the telescope. (Those optical instruments first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608.) Now, advanced ground-based telescopes can produce wonderfully detailed images of those historic remnants. This latest image is from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii and reveals about 10 times more filamentary structures in Pa 30 than have been seen before. This extraordinary detail gives astronomers fresh clues about the unusual explosion and the environment surrounding the star.

"These images give us the clearest picture yet of Pa 30's structure, and it's not what we expected," said Cunningham, whose team published their findings in The Astrophysical Journal. "The filaments are made of chains of tiny knots rather than smooth streaks, providing new constraints on the nature of the space around the star before it exploded and the physical processes that have shaped the expanding ejecta."
The knot-like structures may have resulted from variations in temperature or density in material surrounding the star as debris from the explosion expanded.

Pa 30 contains another unusual feature: a surviving star that sits almost exactly at the center of the remnant. That's highly unusual, because a supernova explosion typically sends stars away from their original positions. It suggests that the original explosion was highly symmetrical, the researchers said.

Furthermore, Pa 30 is thought to be a Type Iax supernova. Unlike standard Type Ia supernovas, which destroy their stars, a Type Iax event is a lower-energy, incomplete explosion of a white dwarf star that can leave behind a remnant known as a "zombie star." It's the only Type Iax supernova ever found.
